newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians fear instability after ex-PM's murder.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians fear instability after ex-PM's murder.

text.p: Bulgarian politicians, shocked by the murder of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, fear more assassinations could follow as the country flounders in crisis.
"This is a demonstrative political killing and the first step has been made," political analyst Kancho Stoichev told Reuters on Thursday.
The Moscow-educated Lukanov, 58, a millionaire businessman and parliamentarian for the ruling Socialists, was found shot dead in front of his Sofia home on Wednesday.

State radio said on Thursday that according to a forensic examination Lukanov was killed with three bullets in the back and one in the head. Investigators declined to give any information on the motives for the killing, the radio added.
Big black headlines in Sofia newspapers asked: "Who will be next?"
"With this act a psychological barrier has been overcome: after the attack on a person such as Lukanov, anybody else could be liquidated," Socialist deputy Georgi Bliznashki told Sega megazine.

The leader of one of the biggest trade unions, Konstantin Trenchev, told a special edition of the newspaper 24 Hours that the murder would "unlock a series (of assassinations) with an unpredictable end".

"Civic peace in Bulgaria has been terminated...and we, the Bulgarians, are all involved," Stoichev said, adding that the country's leaders had direct responsibility for the crisis which had led to such violence.

The small Balkan country of 8.5 million, which ousted its communist rulers in November 1989, is plagued by rising prices, a battered economy and uncertain prospects while suffering a rising crime wave.

Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, expressing concern that the murder was destabilising the country "at the decisive stage of economic reforms" and on the eve of the presidential election, pledged that the government would catch the killers.
He assured the public that no extraordinary measures were necessary but promised to strength social order and legality.

Armed police threw up checkpoints on major roads between the Bulgarian capital and the country's borders. Security measures were tightened at airports, Sofia railway station and border crossing points.
Meanwhile parliament vowed that it would not allow the killing to lead to the declaration of a state of emergency, and vowed the presidential election would take place on October 27 as scheduled.
President Zhelyu Zhelev called for a crackdown on terrorism, organised crime and the mafia.

Lukanov, one of the architects of the downfall of communist dictator Todor Zhivkov in 1989, served as prime minister in 1990 but resigned due to widespread public dissatisfaction with the sluggish pace of reform.
Under his rule, Bulgaria declared a moratorium on $12 billion of foreign debt.
Lukanov, known to be one of the friends of Russia's Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, was one of the founders of a Bulgarian-Russian gas joint stock company, Topenergy.
Politicians said this role troubled his relations with Videnov. In July Lukanov was dropped as Topenergy's board chairman.

In 1992 the public prosecutor launched an inquiry into whether Lukanov misappropriated funds in the 1980s when he was a deputy prime minister. He was stripped of parliamentary rights and detained for six months until the case was dropped.
Parliament called a day of mourning for Friday.
